title: Choosing the Right Channel
body:
Every message begins with a choice that is rarely named: email, short message, or live call. Email suits anything that needs a record, a thoughtful answer, or an attachment, and it respects the reader's time because it can wait. Short messages suit quick coordination, small questions, and confirmations, but they are poor homes for long arguments or sensitive decisions. A call suits anything where tone, speed, or back-and-forth matters, such as resolving a misunderstanding or making a decision together.

Method. Start from the reader's job, not your own convenience. Ask whether the answer needs a permanent record, whether the question is quick or complicated, and whether tone could be misread in plain text. If any two answers point to the same channel, use it. If the message is long, sensitive, or likely to be disputed later, prefer email or a call followed by a written summary, so the decision survives the conversation.

Checklist.

  • Name what you need: an answer, a decision, or a record
  • Pick the channel that fits that need
  • Keep short messages short and emails complete
  • Move to a call when tone is doing the work
  • Confirm decisions in writing afterwards

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Choosing the Right Channel. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: scores: {'email': 5, 'message': 2, 'call': 1}; best channel: email Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Do not use a short message for a decision that affects money, health, or someone's job, and do not send a long email when a two-minute call would settle it. This record does not replace workplace policy: where an employer or organisation names a channel, follow that rule. title: Writing a Clear Email
body:
A clear email answers three questions in its first lines: what this is about, what the reader must do, and by when. The subject line carries the topic and the action, the first sentence carries the request, and the rest carries only the detail the reader needs to act. Readers triage dozens of messages a day, so an email that buries its request in the third paragraph is an email that gets answered late or not at all.

Method. Write the subject as topic plus action, for example a request, a decision, or a date. Open with the request in one sentence, then give the background in short paragraphs, then close with the exact next step and any deadline. Keep attachments named clearly and mentioned in the body, so the reader never has to guess whether something is missing.

Checklist.

  • Subject states topic and action
  • First sentence states the request
  • Background stays short and ordered
  • Attachments are named in the body
  • Close with the next step and deadline

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Writing a Clear Email. Use and limits. Do not use email for urgent matters that need an answer within minutes, and do not hide bad news or a difficult request behind pleasant filler. A clear email is not a cold email: warmth belongs in the greeting and close, not in place of the request. title: The Useful Reply
body:
A useful reply does the reader's next job for them: it answers the question that was actually asked, in the order it was asked, and it says plainly when an answer is not yet known. The most common reply failure is not rudeness but drift, where the reply talks about a nearby topic and leaves the original question untouched, forcing another round of messages. Answering in order, point by point, prevents that drift.

Method. Read the incoming message twice, once for tone and once for questions, and list every question it contains. Answer each in turn, quote briefly where the thread is long, and mark anything deferred with a date for the follow-up. If a question cannot be answered, say so and say what happens next instead of leaving silence that the sender must interpret.

Checklist.

  • List every question in the incoming message
  • Answer in the order asked
  • Quote briefly on long threads
  • Mark deferred answers with a date
  • Say plainly what is not yet known

A reply that promises a date must keep it or send an update before the date passes. title: Group Messages Done Well
body:
A group message is a small public square: everyone included can see it, and everyone included pays attention to it. Good group messages therefore start with inclusion discipline, adding only the people who need the information or the decision, and they keep the thread to one topic so members can mute or leave without losing something else. A group that grows without reason becomes a noisy room that everyone ignores, which defeats its purpose.

Method. Before creating a group, name its purpose and its members, and say in the first message what the group is for. Keep one topic per group where possible, summarise decisions in the thread rather than in side conversations, and move a long discussion to a call or email when the thread stops helping. When the purpose ends, close the group and say so.

Checklist.

  • Name the group's purpose in the first message
  • Include only people who need it
  • One topic per group where possible
  • Summarise decisions in the thread
  • Close the group when its purpose ends

title: Tone in Text
body:
Plain text carries no voice, no face, and no pause, so tone must be built deliberately out of word choice, punctuation, and structure. A short reply that would sound warm in person can read as cold on screen, and a joke that needs a smile can land as an insult without one. Writers who assume their tone is obvious are the writers most often misunderstood, because the reader supplies the tone the writer forgot to include.

Method. Before sending anything sensitive, read it as the recipient would, without your own intended tone in mind. Add the warmth explicitly where it matters, use greetings and closes to frame the message, and avoid sarcasm in any message that could be read by someone outside the intended audience. When a message arrives that reads as hostile, assume a missing tone before assuming a hostile intent, and reply to the content rather than the imagined tone.

Checklist.

  • Read the message as the recipient would
  • Add warmth explicitly where it matters
  • Use greetings and closes as framing
  • Avoid sarcasm in shareable messages
  • Reply to content, not imagined tone

Where a conversation has already turned tense, moving to a call is usually better than composing a more careful text. title: Voice Notes With Care
body:
A voice note carries tone that text cannot, which makes it ideal for encouragement, explanation, and anything where warmth matters. It is a poor choice for information the listener must search later, such as an address, a date, or a list of steps, because audio cannot be skimmed. The rule is simple: voice for feeling and explanation, text for facts the listener will need again.

Method. Keep voice notes short, ideally under two minutes, and open with the point so the listener knows whether to listen now or later. Follow a voice note that contains facts with a short text summary of those facts, and never send a voice note that demands an immediate spoken reply from someone who may be in a place where they cannot listen or speak. Respect the listener's setting as much as your own convenience.

Checklist.

  • Open with the point
  • Keep notes short
  • Follow facts with a text summary
  • Never demand an immediate spoken reply
  • Respect the listener's setting

title: Setting Up a Video Call
body:
Most video call failures happen before the call starts: a link that was never tested, a time that was never confirmed in both time zones, or a device whose camera or microphone was never checked. A short setup routine removes almost all of these failures, and it costs less than a minute when done in advance. The routine matters most for calls with people who are less confident with technology, where a failed start can end the conversation entirely.

Method. Send the link, the date, the time with its time zone, and a one-line purpose in a single message, so nothing must be hunted across threads. Test the link, camera, and microphone before the call, charge or plug in the device, and join two minutes early. Tell the other person how to reach you if the call fails, by a message or a phone number, so a technical failure becomes a brief detour rather than a lost meeting.

Checklist.

  • Link, date, time, and time zone in one message
  • One-line purpose
  • Test link, camera, and microphone
  • Join two minutes early
  • Share a fallback contact method

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Setting Up a Video Call. Use and limits. Do not assume everyone shares your time zone or your software, and do not send a link without a time or a time without a link. Where a participant needs accessibility support, ask in advance what helps, such as captions or a dial-in option, rather than discovering the need mid-call. title: Looking and Sounding Good on Video
body:
A video call is judged first by whether the other person can see and hear you clearly, and only second by what you say. Good lighting means light on your face rather than behind you, good sound means a quiet room and a microphone close enough to catch speech without echo, and a good background means nothing distracting or private is visible behind you. These three fixes cost nothing and change how seriously a call is taken.

Method. Face a window or a lamp, never sit with a bright window behind you, and raise the camera to eye level so the other person sees your face rather than your ceiling. Mute when you are not speaking in a group call, unmute before you speak, and check what is visible behind you, including papers, screens, and other people. Speak a little more slowly than in person, because call audio compresses and delays speech.

Checklist.

  • Light on your face, not behind you
  • Camera at eye level
  • Mute when not speaking in groups
  • Check the background for private items
  • Speak a little more slowly

title: Running a Small Video Meeting
body:
A small video meeting succeeds when everyone leaves knowing what was decided and who does what next. That outcome comes from a short agenda sent in advance, a chair who keeps the conversation on that agenda, and notes taken during the meeting rather than reconstructed afterwards. Without those three, a meeting becomes a conversation that must be repeated, because no one can prove what was agreed.

Method. Send an agenda with a purpose, a short list of items, and a time for each, and start on time whether or not everyone has arrived. Give each item a decision or a next step before moving on, invite quiet participants by name rather than by general appeal, and close by reading back decisions and owners. Send the notes the same day, while memory is fresh.

Checklist.

  • Agenda sent in advance with times
  • Start on time
  • One decision or next step per item
  • Invite quiet participants by name
  • Read back decisions and owners at the close

title: The Follow-Up Summary
body:
A follow-up summary turns a conversation into a record that everyone involved can check. It names what was decided, who owns each next step, and by when, and it is sent promptly while the conversation is still fresh in everyone's mind. Without it, each participant leaves with a slightly different memory of the same call, and the differences surface later as disagreements about what was agreed.

Method. Write the summary the same day, keep it to the decisions and next steps rather than a transcript, and send it to everyone who was on the call, including anyone who was absent but affected. Invite corrections with a short window for replies, so a mistaken summary is fixed while it is still easy to fix. File the summary where the decision's thread lives, not in a separate inbox.

Checklist.

  • Decisions named plainly
  • Each next step has an owner and date
  • Sent the same day
  • Corrections invited with a window
  • Filed with the decision's thread

title: Response-Time Boundaries
body:
Response-time boundaries protect both sides of a conversation: the sender knows when to expect a reply, and the receiver is not expected to answer at all hours. Without stated boundaries, every unread message feels urgent and every delayed reply feels like neglect, even when neither is true. Stating a simple expectation, such as replies within one working day for email and sooner for urgent calls, removes most of that friction.

Method. State your own response times plainly, for example in a signature, a status message, or a first reply, and respect the boundaries others state. Separate urgent from non-urgent by channel: a call signals urgency, a message does not, and treating every message as urgent destroys the signal. Use do-not-disturb settings during rest, focus, and family time, and tell regular contacts where urgent matters should go instead.

Checklist.

  • State your response times plainly
  • Separate urgent from non-urgent by channel
  • Respect boundaries others state
  • Use do-not-disturb during rest and focus
  • Name where urgent matters should go

title: Communicating Across Time Zones
body:
Working across time zones fails most often on small details: a time given without its zone, a deadline that means Friday in one place and Saturday in another, or a meeting set at an hour that is reasonable for one side and the middle of the night for the other. The fix is to name the zone every time, to share times in both zones where it helps, and to rotate inconvenient hours rather than always asking the same side to bear them.

Method. Always write times with their zone, and for shared deadlines write the date and time in each participant's zone. When scheduling, check the other side's working hours before proposing, offer two or three options rather than one, and rotate early or late slots across the group over time. For deadlines, state the zone the deadline is judged in, so no one discovers too late that their Friday was already someone else's Saturday.

Checklist.

  • Name the time zone every time
  • Share deadline times in each zone
  • Offer two or three meeting options
  • Rotate inconvenient hours fairly
  • State the zone a deadline is judged in

title: Accessible Everyday Communication
body:
Accessible communication means a message can be received by people with different hearing, vision, language, and device needs. Captions make calls usable for people who cannot hear well or cannot play sound aloud; plain words make messages usable for readers with less fluency or less time; text alternatives make voice and image content usable for people who cannot hear or see it. Accessibility is not an extra audience, it is the same audience with its real range of needs recognised.

Method. Turn captions on for group calls and share a written summary afterwards, so the call is usable with sound off or hearing difficulty. Write in plain words and short sentences for important instructions, describe images that carry meaning, and offer a text alternative for every voice note that contains facts. Ask participants what helps them rather than guessing, and build the answer into the routine rather than treating it as a one-time favour.

Checklist.

  • Captions on for group calls
  • Written summary after calls
  • Plain words for important instructions
  • Text alternative for voice facts
  • Ask participants what helps

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Accessible Everyday Communication. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: needs met: 3 of 3; accessible: True Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Do not treat accessibility as a favour that can be withdrawn when busy, and do not rely on automatic captions alone for decisions that matter: check the caption record against the summary. Where a participant's need is not met by the standard routine, adapt the routine rather than asking the participant to adapt to it. title: Correcting a Mis-Sent Message
body:
Everyone sends a message to the wrong person, with the wrong attachment, or with a wording they regret, and the repair matters more than the mistake. A good correction is fast, plain, and complete: it says what was wrong, gives the right information, and apologises without excuses or blame. A slow or evasive correction lets the wrong version spread, and by the time it is fixed, the fix must chase copies that have already been forwarded.

Method. Act as soon as the error is noticed: send a correction in the same thread or channel, state plainly what was wrong and what is right, and apologise briefly. If the message reached the wrong person, tell them it was not intended for them and ask them to delete it, without demanding or threatening. If the error affected a decision, follow the correction with a check that the right version is now the one being used.

Checklist.

  • Correct in the same thread or channel
  • State what was wrong and what is right
  • Apologise briefly without excuses
  • Ask wrong recipients to delete it
  • Check the right version is now in use

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Correcting a Mis-Sent Message. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: sent to: 2; wrong recipients: ['Ben']; correction needed: True Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Do not delete a mistaken message silently and hope no one noticed, since silence leaves the wrong version standing, and do not over-apologise in a way that makes the correction harder to find. Where a mis-sent message contained private information, treat the privacy consequence seriously and seek advice if the exposure is significant. title: Keeping a Record of Decisions
body:
Decisions made in messages are easily lost, because a chat thread scrolls away and an inbox buries the decisive message under newer ones. Keeping a record means moving each decision out of the stream and into a place where it can be found later: a short note naming the decision, the date, the people involved, and where the supporting messages live. The record does not need to be elaborate; it needs to be findable.

Method. After a decision, write a one-paragraph note with the decision, the date, the owners, and a pointer to the thread or email where it was made. Keep notes in one place per project or household, use consistent titles so they can be searched, and review them when a related decision comes up, so new decisions build on old ones instead of contradicting them unknowingly. Delete or archive records that are no longer needed, so the archive stays trustworthy.

Checklist.

  • One-paragraph note per decision
  • Decision, date, owners, and pointer
  • One place per project or household
  • Consistent titles for searching
  • Review before related decisions

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Keeping a Record of Decisions. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: records kept: 2; all have dates: True; latest decision: catering Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Do not keep private messages verbatim in a shared record without considering who can read it, and do not keep records that the law or an organisation's policy requires to be deleted. A record that cannot be found is no record at all, so findability matters more than completeness. title: Checking Before Acting on an Urgent Request
body:
Urgent requests that arrive by message deserve a pause, because urgency is the easiest feeling to manufacture and the hardest to check while feeling it. A genuine urgent request survives a check; a false one depends on the check not happening. The safe habit is to verify through a separate channel you already trust, such as calling a known number or asking in person, before sending money, sharing credentials, or changing an account on the strength of a message alone.

Method. When a message demands immediate action involving money, credentials, or account changes, stop and contact the supposed sender through a number or address you already hold, not one supplied in the suspicious message. Ask whether they sent it, and wait for a clear answer before acting. If the sender cannot be reached, treat the request as unverified and do not act on it; a genuine sender can resend or confirm, while an acted-on false request often cannot be undone.

Checklist.

  • Pause on urgent money or credential requests
  • Contact the sender through a known channel
  • Never use contact details from the message itself
  • Wait for a clear confirmation
  • If unverified, do not act
